subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: using AI as a tutor by asking for explanations [Action]
passage:
Monday. Deepika stared at x² + 5x + 6 = 0 for twenty minutes. The textbook's steps might as well have been in another language. She was close to tears when her brother Eshaan said, “Ask the AI to explain it like you're twelve.” She did, and it broke the steps into small pieces: find two numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5.
Wednesday. She asked for five practice questions and solved them all on paper before looking at the answers. Three right, two wrong. She asked why the wrong ones were wrong.
Saturday. Class test. Deepika solved four equations with no phone in sight and got three right. She told Eshaan, “It didn't do it for me. It sat next to me while I did it.”

qa.q: How many practice questions did Deepika ask for?
qa.a: Deepika asked for five practice questions.

qa.q: How did Deepika feel on Monday?
qa.a: Deepika felt frustrated and close to tears after twenty minutes with no progress.

qa.q: What could Deepika do if the tool's explanation is still unclear?
qa.a: Deepika could ask her teacher or ask the tool to explain in a different way, since another route may click when the first does not.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see her progress?
qa.a: Eshaan is probably pleased, since his suggestion helped, and her sentence about the tool sitting next to her shows she did the work.

grounding: A teen stuck on quadratic equations asks an AI to explain the steps simply and give practice questions, then solves them herself and checks afterwards.

passage: You're stuck on quadratics too, Damini? Let me tell you about Vandana from the third floor. Last winter she came to me in tears, beta. Forty years I taught maths, and I could see she'd been copying steps without knowing why. She showed me her phone: she had asked one of these AI tools to solve her homework. I said, "Ask it something else. Ask it to explain like you're twelve." So she typed, "Explain factorising quadratics in simpler words, one step at a time. Don't give me answers." It explained, then gave her five practice questions. She solved them at my dining table with a pencil and checked each one after. Two were wrong. Both times she found her own mistake, a sign error. Your Nani may be old, Damini, but I know this: that tool is only as good as the question you ask it.

qa.q: How many practice questions did the AI give Vandana?
qa.a: It gave her five practice questions.

qa.q: What was Vandana feeling when she first came to Nani?
qa.a: Vandana was upset and frustrated, in tears after copying steps she didn't understand.

qa.q: What turning point in the story changed how Vandana used the tool?
qa.a: Asking it to explain in simpler words and give practice questions instead of answers, then solving them alone and checking afterwards.

qa.q: How did Nani see Vandana's first use of the tool?
qa.a: Nani, a retired maths teacher, could see Vandana had been copying steps without understanding, and nudged her toward asking better questions.

grounding: Shows a teen stuck on quadratics asking an AI to explain the steps simply and give practice questions, then solving them herself and checking afterwards.

subtopic: Using AI tools for learning without cheating
subtype: Approach: using AI as a tutor by asking for explanations [Action]
passage: The unit test was at nine the next morning, and at eight-thirty that night the power went out across Himani's colony in Jaipur. Her laptop was dead; her phone had twenty percent battery and very little data left. One kind of question still beat her: the quadratic formula problems. Her brother Saurabh held up an emergency lamp. "Just ask the AI to solve the worksheet." Himani shook her head. "Then I'll be stuck again at nine tomorrow." Instead she typed one short message: "Explain the quadratic formula in simple words. Then give me three practice questions without answers." She read the explanation twice, switched off her data to save battery, and worked the three questions on paper by lamplight. When the power returned at ten, she checked her answers. Two right. The third had a wrong sign, and now she could see exactly where.

qa.q: How much battery did Himani's phone have?
qa.a: Her phone had twenty percent battery.

qa.q: Why did Himani refuse to have the AI solve the worksheet?
qa.a: Himani was worried about being stuck again in the test the next morning, so she wanted to understand, not just collect answers.

qa.q: What else could Himani do with the one wrong answer?
qa.a: She could ask for two more questions of the same kind, or show it to her teacher, so the sign error doesn't repeat.

qa.q: How might Saurabh see Himani's choice?
qa.a: Saurabh offered the quick shortcut, so he may be surprised she chose the slower way, but it shows him how to learn from the tool instead of copying.

grounding: Illustrates a teen, with little battery and time, asking an AI for a simple explanation and practice questions on quadratics and solving them herself.
